gallery.filename: Hukkala family, Keweenaw National Historical Park, 1927. (56a6bc86e58f431d898ebbdc829f4694).jpg
gallery.title: File:Hukkala family, Keweenaw National Historical Park, 1927. (56a6bc86e58f431d898ebbdc829f4694).jpg
gallery.description:
Gabriel Hukkala was born in Vaasa, Finland in 1866 and immigrated to the United States with his brother, John, around 1890. He landed in Marquette and then moved to Calumet, working as a tailor. In 1898 he married fellow Finnish-immigrant, Margareta Ervasti, in Calumet. Finnish Apostolic Lutheran Pastor A.L. Heideman officiated the ceremony. The couple had five children while living in Calumet, Laurium and Centennial Heights. By 1910 Gabriel had his own tailor shop in South Range, where the family also lived. Their son, Gabriel Jr., later became a professional staff artist for The Chicago Daily News. After a stroke left his right side paralyzed, he demonstrated his 'sisu' by learning to paint with his left hand. Sisu cannot be translated into the English language but roughly means, stoic determination, bravery and resilience. Gabriel Senior's family members were laid to rest at South Range's Mountain View Cemetery. Gabriel Junior's family are interred at the Rosehill Cemetery in Chicago. Photo courtesy of family.
Keywords: immigrant; immigrants; finland; historical; black and white; calumet

gallery.filename: Churches of Oak and Seventh Streets (3a432ea8-1dd8-b71b-0b82-b6fee0fbfe04).jpg
gallery.title: File:Churches of Oak and Seventh Streets (3a432ea8-1dd8-b71b-0b82-b6fee0fbfe04).jpg
gallery.description:
Historical image overlaid onto a present day photo
Many of Calumet's churches are #MissingintheCopperCountry, as a scene photographed from the southeast corner of Oak and Seventh Streets in 1907 and then in 2014 demonstrates. St.Paul the Apostle Catholic Church (standing, formerly St. Joseph's, left) once neighbored the Red Jacket Congregational Church and St. Anthony of Padua Polish Catholic Church (l-r).
The Red Jacket Congregational church united with Calumet's First Congregational Church in the 1920s and its building was demolished in the 1930s. St. Anthony's also maintained a school and convent; with falling numbers, their congregation united with nearby St. Joseph's in 1928. The former St. Anthony's was later demolished, although its brick convent and cement block rectory still front Seventh Street on either side of the location where the church once stood.

gallery.filename: According to Edwin Hulbert, who discovered the Calumet Conglomerate Lode, the Calumet Hotel was the first building built in the (3baff558-1dd8-b71b-0be6-eefbdfed8969).jpg
gallery.title: File:According to Edwin Hulbert, who discovered the Calumet Conglomerate Lode, the Calumet Hotel was the first building built in the (3baff558-1dd8-b71b-0be6-eefbdfed8969).jpg
gallery.description:
Historical photo overlaid onto a present day photo.
According to Edwin Hulbert, who discovered the Calumet Conglomerate Lode, the Calumet Hotel was the first building built in the Calumet area. The oldest portion of the building was a log dwelling constructed ca. 1864. Being the only dwelling in the area, it served those who worked in the initial exploration of the Hulbert, Calumet, and Hecla Mining Company properties, as well as visiting potential investors. It was added on to a number of times over the years; eventually it was known as the Calumet House, and then as the Calumet Hotel. The hotel offered accommodations and meals for visitors to the area as well as temporary offices and show rooms (or "sample rooms") for local and out-of-town businesses. It was located at the intersection of Calumet Avenue (US-41) and School Street.
The Calumet Hotel was destroyed by fire on January 27, 1918. Believed to have started in a garbage can behind the building, the fire ate at the hotel and many of the guests' belongings while most of the furnishings were hastily removed. The hotel burned well into the night before firemen from four departments were able to extinguish the blaze. After the fire, the ruins of the building were soon removed. Thus Calumet's earliest building and first hostelry went #MissingintheCopperCountry.

gallery.filename: Diamond Match is America's oldest operating match company. It was active in Ontonagon County for many years, by 1883 employing (3c038899-1dd8-b71b-0b43-ccae52fdf596).jpg
gallery.title: File:Diamond Match is America's oldest operating match company. It was active in Ontonagon County for many years, by 1883 employing (3c038899-1dd8-b71b-0b43-ccae52fdf596).jpg
gallery.description:
Historical photo overlaid onto a present day photo
Diamond Match is America's oldest operating match company. It was active in Ontonagon County for many years, by 1883 employing over 500 men at lumber camps in and around Ontonagon County. West of the mouth of the Ontonagon River stood its lumberyards, mills and manufacturing facilities. The company store stood on River Street in the village of Ontonagon, across the slough from the mills. Originally built by Horace H. Rich and the Ontonagon Lumber Company, the store was taken over by the Diamond Match Company when it took over the lumberyard and area timberlands. Measuring 110' x 110', it featured an elevator and skylights to showcase its $20,000.00 of inventory that included a wide variety of goods, from foodstuffs to furniture.
Across the slough from the store, the lumberyard was stacked high with pine set to dry before being made into matches. A forest fire to the west of the Ontonagon River would become the most devastating fire in Ontonagon's history when lumber began smoldering near the Diamond Match Company's mills. On August 25, 1896, strong winds carried the fire across the river to the village, where it destroyed nearly 340 buildings, sparing only 12. Nearly two thousand people were made homeless and left to rebuild.
The company store went #MissingintheCopperCountry alongside most of pre-1896 Ontonagon. Diamond Match tapered off its Ontonagon operations over the following years, never rebuilding the company's mills or store.

gallery.filename: Beside Calumet's Michigan House is a small parking lot bordering Ash Lane (the alley). It's hard to fathom that two structures (3d60ead5-1dd8-b71b-0b37-d3bcf0706134).jpg
gallery.title: File:Beside Calumet's Michigan House is a small parking lot bordering Ash Lane (the alley). It's hard to fathom that two structures (3d60ead5-1dd8-b71b-0b37-d3bcf0706134).jpg
gallery.description:
Historical photo overlaid onto a present day photo
Beside Calumet's Michigan House is a small parking lot bordering Ash Lane (the alley). It's hard to fathom that two structures stood between the Hotel Michigan and the alley for most of the village's past. Two dwellings occupied this small space along bustling Oak Street in downtown Red Jacket. The one beside the Michigan House became a laundry and later a confectionery, while the other remained a private residence.
Still standing in 1942, today they're #MissingintheCopperCountry.
